c1.story:
Every Indian growth story eventually becomes a steel story. The metro line outside your office, the expressway you drove last weekend, the car in its parking slot, the washing machine at home, the gas pipeline running under a field in Gujarat: all of it is steel, rolled, bent, welded or coated. India is now the world's second-largest steel producer, behind only China, and it is the one large economy where steel demand is still growing at a brisk clip year after year.

So owning a steel stock should be simple, right? Buy the demand story and wait. Not quite. The phrase steel company covers four businesses that make money in four different ways, and they react to the same headline in very different ways.

The first door is the giant integrated mill: Tata Steel at Jamshedpur and Kalinganagar, JSW at Vijayanagar, SAIL at Bhilai and Bokaro, Jindal Steel at Angul. These melt iron ore with coking coal in blast furnaces the height of a high-rise and sell flat steel, coils and sheets, to carmakers and appliance makers. The second door is the secondary producer in the mineral belt of Chhattisgarh and Odisha: sponge iron, induction furnaces, rebar for construction, often with its own power plant and, in the best cases, its own iron ore. Lloyds Metals with its mine at Surjagarh in Gadchiroli is the textbook example of how much owning the rock can be worth.

The third door is stainless and specialty: Jindal Stainless, Usha Martin's wire ropes, Gravita's recycled metals. These sell metal for what it does rather than what it weighs. And the fourth door does not make steel at all. Jindal SAW, Ratnamani and Bansal Wire buy coil or wire rod and turn it into pipes, tubes and wire against orders, charging a fee for the conversion.

A steel price headline is good news, bad news or no news, depending on which door you are standing behind.

When Chinese coil prices jump, door one celebrates, door two shrugs, door three watches nickel, and door four mostly checks whether its customers will delay orders.
c1.read:
Four tiles, four business models. Read each tile from top to bottom, then compare the bars across the row.

  • The name and the line under it describe the furnace and the customer: blast furnaces and flat steel for the majors, sponge iron and rebar for the secondary mills, stainless for the specialists, and order-based conversion for the pipe and wire makers.
  • The tickers are listed names that sit mostly behind that door. Click any of them to open its stock page. Notice that JINDALSTEL sits with the majors while LLOYDSME sits with the secondary producers, even though both are really ore stories at heart.
  • The profit bar is the one to stare at. Three of the four doors show medium, which is unusual: in most commodity industries the producers sit at low. Steel producers keep a middling share because India's demand is strong and a duty wall now shields them, but they still hand a lot back to Queensland coal sellers and to Chinese price-setters. The converters show high, because once a pipe maker is certified for a gas pipeline or a refinery, the customer rarely shops around on price alone.
  • The bet line tells you what you are really buying: a spread, a construction cycle plus ore, a niche price, or an order book.

Before you read anything else about a steel name, place it on one of these tiles. A company that straddles two, say a mill with a big pipe arm, should be valued as two businesses.

c2.story:
Picture a kitchen that starts in the red earth of Odisha and ends on a construction site in Pune. At station one, iron ore is dug out of the ground in Odisha, Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand and Karnataka. India is blessed with ore. What it lacks is the other ingredient, good coking coal, and so the second half of station one arrives by ship from Australia, with Russian cargoes growing in recent years, landing at Paradip, Dhamra, Gangavaram and Vizag on the east coast.

Station two prepares the iron. Fine ore is rolled into pellets and baked, or turned into sponge iron with gas or thermal coal. This is where a lot of the secondary producers earn their living, and where many unlisted units in Raipur and Rourkela crowd in alongside them.

Station three is the dramatic one: melting. Blast furnaces turn ore and coke into liquid iron, which becomes steel; electric and induction furnaces do the same with scrap and sponge iron. Station four rolls and finishes: slabs become coil, billets become rebar, coil becomes pipe, stainless becomes a sink. Station five is the customer, a builder, a carmaker, a railway, a city gas company.

Now notice the shape of India's position. Indian listed companies dominate the middle three stations. The trouble is at both ends. Upstream, a few Australian mines and the state ore miner NMDC set the price of the inputs. Downstream, the final price of the product is set not in India but in China, which makes about half the world's steel.

That is why steel in India is a sandwich business. In 2021, when coal was fine and Chinese prices were high, the filling was thick. In 2022, coking coal more than doubled after Russia invaded Ukraine and the sandwich got thin from below. In 2023 and 2024 China's property crash pushed its surplus abroad and the bread got squeezed from above.
c2.read:
Read the diagram in two passes: the station boxes left to right, then the two rows of bands underneath.

The five boxes run from the mine on the left to the user on the right. Each box tells you what happens there and who does it. Watch how the cast changes: NMDC, the state miners, captive mines and Australian coal on the left; pellet and sponge iron makers next; then the big melters; then the rolling mills and converters; and the builders and carmakers at the end. The boxes coloured as Indian listed are stations two, three and four.

The first band row tells you who holds each station. The first cell is marked as a rival, Australian coal and NMDC: that is the industry admitting that it does not control its own most important cost. The next three cells say India listed. The last cell, builders and autos, is the customer.

The second band row shows China standing at the producing stations alongside Indian companies, with the word World under the customer station. That row is the reason a steel price in Mumbai moves with a steel price in Tangshan: China does not need to sell in India to set the price here, it only needs to be able to.

The practical use: trace any news item to its station. A Queensland cyclone or a coal-export ban hits station one, and you should expect blast-furnace margins at station three to feel it within a quarter. A Chinese export surge hits the price at station four and five. A new rebar order from a highway project starts at station five and flows backwards.

c3.story:
Ask who buys Indian steel and the instinctive answer is carmakers. They are important, and they buy the fanciest grades, the cold-rolled and galvanised sheet that becomes a door panel. But they are not the biggest customer. That title belongs to the humble construction site, which takes well over half of Indian steel through rebar, wire rod and structural sections.

This matters because construction demand marches to a different drummer. A car sale depends on a household's mood and a loan rate. A rebar order depends on whether a builder has launched a tower, whether a state has paid its highway contractor, whether the railway has released funds for a new line. Since the pandemic, the government's own capital spending has been the single most important engine of Indian steel demand: roads, railways, metro systems, ports, airports and the water pipes of the Jal Jeevan Mission, launched in 2019 to bring a tap to every rural household.

Pipes are a mini-story of their own. The Jal Jeevan Mission was a bonanza for ductile iron and spiral-welded pipe makers. The national gas grid and city gas networks need large-diameter line pipe. Refineries and power plants need seamless and stainless tubes that can take heat and pressure. That is why the converters' fortunes are tied to project pipelines rather than to the coil price.

And then there are exports, the release valve. When Indian demand is soft, mills push hot-rolled coil to Europe, the Gulf and Southeast Asia. When Chinese prices are low, that valve is shut, and when Europe's carbon border tax bites, a slice of it stays shut for good.

In India, the finance minister's capex line moves more steel than the car showroom does.
c3.read:
Each tile is one customer group. Read it in three lines: who buys, what they buy, and what moves them.

  • Construction and real estate and Infrastructure sit first for a reason: together they are the bulk of demand. Their third lines read housing starts, cement volumes, interest rates, and government capex. If you watch nothing else, watch these.
  • Automobiles and Consumer durables buy the premium flat products. They are smaller in tonnes but bigger in margin per tonne, which is why the flat-steel majors care about them more than the tonnage suggests.
  • Capital goods buys plates and alloy steel, and moves with private capex and defence orders.
  • Oil, gas and water pipelines is the converters' tile. Its third line, Jal Jeevan funding, the gas grid, refinery capex, is effectively the order book of door four.
  • Exports is the valve. Its third line names the two forces that open and close it: Chinese export prices and European rules.

One way to use the grid: map each company you own onto the tiles. A long-steel producer is almost entirely on the first two. A flat-steel major spreads across autos, durables, capital goods and exports. A pipe maker sits on one tile. Then cross-check with the so-what line underneath: if construction and infra are well over half of demand, the Union Budget's capex number is a steel earnings indicator.

c4.story:
Strip a steel mill to its bones and it is a spread business. It buys ore and coking coal, it sells steel, and it lives in the gap between the two. Analysts compress that gap into one number, EBITDA per tonne: operating profit, before depreciation, interest and tax, divided by tonnes shipped. It is the steel industry's pulse, and across a cycle it can swing by half.

Here is how it moves. The selling side, realisation per tonne, follows Chinese export prices with a lag of a few weeks to a quarter, because Indian buyers can always threaten to import. The cost side is dominated by coking coal for blast-furnace mills, priced in dollars off Australian benchmarks and notoriously jumpy. A cyclone in Queensland, a mine flood, a surge in Chinese buying, and the coal bill can double in months, as it did in 2022. Because coal bought today is melted next quarter, there is always a lag, and that lag decides whether a quarter looks like a feast or a famine.

Then come the lines that separate survivors from casualties. Interest is a big one. Indian steel has a painful memory here: in the bust of the last decade, Essar Steel, Bhushan Steel and several others collapsed under debt and went through the insolvency courts, ending up with ArcelorMittal and Nippon Steel, Tata Steel and JSW. Debt-funded capacity built at the top of a cycle is how steel companies die. Depreciation jumps when a new blast furnace is lit, and capex is enormous because every major is expanding at once.

Finally, overseas subsidiaries. Tata Steel's European plants, bought with Corus in 2007, have swung group profits for most of the time since, and the shutdown of its Port Talbot blast furnaces in Wales in 2024 is a reminder that a foreign acquisition can be a decade-long earnings story of its own. JSW's American plants have played a similar, smaller role.
c4.read:
The two charts walk one hundred rupees of sales down to what is left, first for an integrated major, then for a pipe and wire converter. Read each chart left to right.

  • The first bar is the full hundred rupees.
  • The input bar is iron ore and coking coal for the major, and bought coil or wire rod for the converter. The major's input bite is a little over half its sales; the converter's is roughly two-thirds. That surprises people: the converter pays more for its raw material because its raw material is someone else's finished steel.
  • The opex bar is power, people and freight. The major spends more here, a quarter of sales, because running a blast furnace, a coke oven and a rolling mill is a power-hungry, people-heavy affair.
  • The depreciation and interest bar is where the business models really part ways. The major's bar is far taller, because a steel plant is a mountain of capital and usually of debt. The converter's is small: a pipe mill is cheap by comparison.
  • The last bar is what remains. In these mid-cycle shapes the two end up with about the same slice, a tenth of sales, but they get there by opposite routes: the major pays less for inputs and more for its plant, the converter the reverse. And the converter keeps its slice more reliably, because its margin is a conversion fee and not a bet on the coil price.

These are illustrative shapes, not any company's accounts; hover a bar for the rupee amount.

Below, the line list shows what to watch. EBITDA per tonne, coking coal cost, realisation, capex and interest all carry a yes. Depreciation, working capital and overseas subsidiaries are sometimes: big when a furnace starts, a price spikes or Europe has a bad year, quiet otherwise.

c5.story:
Steel is one of the most honestly cyclical industries in the market, and the last six years have been a textbook cycle squeezed into fast-forward.

Start in 2019: a sluggish Indian economy, weak autos and real estate, thin margins. Then the pandemic, and the most violent upswing in living memory. Governments everywhere spent on recovery, China held back its own output and exports, and coil prices ran to records. Indian mills earned their best profit per tonne ever, and they did something unusual with the money: they paid down debt instead of immediately building new furnaces.

The peak arrived in 2022. Russia's invasion of Ukraine sent coking coal more than doubling. In May, the government slapped an export duty on steel to cool domestic prices, cutting off the export valve just as costs spiked. It withdrew the duty in November, but by then margins had rolled over.

Then came the bust of 2023 and 2024, and it came from China. Its property sector, the single biggest steel consumer on the planet, was in a slow-motion collapse after the Evergrande default. Chinese mills did not cut output to match; they exported the surplus at whatever price cleared. Imports into India hit records, domestic coil fell to its lowest in years, and margins shrank even though Indian demand was growing strongly. That is the cruel part of steel: you can have the best demand in the world and still lose money if your neighbour has nowhere to put his.

The turn came through policy. A provisional safeguard duty on flat steel imports arrived in April 2025, and at the end of that year the finance ministry made it definitive for three years, stepping down a little each year. Prices firmed, coking coal was cheap, and the clock moved into an early up-cycle. The wall is the support, and also the risk.
c5.read:
Three pieces work together: the clock, the timeline beside it, and the four hands below.

The clock has four arcs running clockwise from the top: boom, peak, bust and bottom. The years under each arc are when the last cycle passed through that phase: boom in 2020 and 2021, peak in 2022, bust across 2023 and 2024, bottom in 2025. The arrow from the centre points to today. For steel it sits just short of twelve o'clock, at the very end of the bottom arc, tipping into the boom arc: an early up-cycle. Hover any arc for what defined it.

The timeline retells the cycle year by year, colour-coded by tone. Notice the rhythm: a bust year in 2019, the boom, a neutral peak, the long bust, a neutral bottom, and the latest entry marked now. The now entry lists the three supports of today's position: the extended safeguard duty, India's demand, and new capacity, with China's exports named as the cap.

The four hands let you move the arrow yourself.

  • Chinese steel export price: low and stable, with no arrow. This is the missing ingredient. If it rises, the ceiling lifts and the cycle is turning for real.
  • Domestic hot-rolled coil price: firm behind the duty, arrow up.
  • Coking coal price: moderate, no arrow. A spike here would squeeze blast-furnace margins a quarter later.
  • Steel imports into India: falling, arrow up for the industry, because the duty is working. Watch for a rebound through countries not covered by the duty.

Two good hands, two neutral ones: that is what early up-cycle looks like in practice.

c6.story:
An Indian steel mill's quarter is decided by a surprisingly international cast. A property developer in Guangdong deciding not to start a tower. A coal planner in Queensland watching the cyclone forecast. A trade official in Delhi drafting a duty notification. A budget officer in North Block deciding how much the railways get.

Four dials carry the heaviest weight, and they are worth understanding as a set. Chinese export prices are the ceiling: no Indian mill can charge much above the landed price of Chinese coil for long. Coking coal is the floor of costs for every blast furnace. Government capital spending is the volume engine for long steel and pipes. And trade protection, the safeguard and anti-dumping duties, decides how far below the Chinese ceiling the Indian price is allowed to fall. When all four point the right way, as they did in 2021, steel mills print money. When the first two turn against you at once, as in 2022 and 2023, no amount of Indian demand saves the quarter.

Then there are the two-faced dials. A higher iron ore price is a cost for a mill that buys its ore and income for one that mines its own; this is why the market has re-rated the ore-owning names so sharply since the 2020 lease auctions. A weaker rupee raises the coal import bill while making exports more competitive.

And the slow dials. Interest rates matter for balance sheets that carry heavy debt. Europe's carbon border tax, which started charging in 2026, quietly makes Indian blast-furnace steel dearer in one of its key export outlets. It is a small dial today, but it is the one that could grow.
c6.read:
Each row is one dial. Read across in four steps: the dial, the channel, what a rise does, and the weight.

  • Channel is how the dial reaches profits. For steel the channels sort neatly into price ceiling, input cost, volume and protection.
  • A rise does carries an arrow. Green up means a rise helps: Chinese prices, government capex, trade protection, domestic output and auto production. Red down means a rise hurts: coking coal, interest rates and the EU carbon tax. The diamond means it cuts both ways: iron ore and the rupee, where the answer depends on whether the company owns ore or exports.
  • Weight runs from one to three dots. Four rows carry three dots, more than most industries: Chinese prices, coking coal, government capex and trade protection. That tells you steel has more than one master.

The latest column shows a live reading where the dial maps to a series we track. Several steel dials use proxies: the Nifty Metal index stands in for Chinese prices, the Nifty Infra index for government capex, the core-sector steel and iron ore indices for output, the Nifty Auto index for car demand. Proxies are imperfect, so treat them as a direction check. Coking coal and trade protection show a dash: follow those through the news and the companies' quarterly commentary.

The fastest way to use this table is to scan the three-dot rows first, then check whether the green and red arrows among them are currently pointing for or against the industry.

c7.story:
If Indian steel demand is so strong, why don't Indian steel companies simply grow forever? Because seven things get in the way, and two of them never leave.

The first is Chinese overcapacity. China built a steel industry sized for a property boom that has now ended. Its home demand is shrinking, its mills are reluctant to close because they employ whole towns, and the surplus goes abroad. As long as that surplus exists, every Indian price has a lid on it. The second permanent problem is coking coal. India has plenty of coal, but very little of the right kind for blast furnaces, and what it has is high in ash. So the most important input for most Indian steel arrives on a ship, priced in dollars, from a handful of Australian mines.

Then there is the bottleneck that has become a moat: iron ore leases. For years, ore mining was a mess of illegal-mining scandals and court bans in Goa and Karnataka. Many merchant leases expired in March 2020 and were re-auctioned, with winners promising large shares of revenue to the state. Companies that already owned ore, or won it cheaply, now have a cost edge that is very hard to copy.

The killer bottleneck is debt. Steel capex is huge, and steel cycles are fast. The last decade's wreckage, with Essar, Bhushan and others in insolvency court, happened because companies borrowed at the top and could not service the debt at the bottom. Every major is building again now. The question for each one is whether its balance sheet can survive a bust that arrives before the new furnace fills.

Steel does not usually kill companies with weak demand. It kills them with debt taken on at the wrong moment.

Add policy swings, carbon intensity and the annual squeeze on rail rakes and port berths, and you have the full list.
c7.read:
Each row is one bottleneck, with why it bites and a severity label. The label tells you which kind of risk you are holding.

  • Structural rows are Chinese overcapacity and coking coal dependence. They do not go away. They set the ceiling on returns for the whole industry and belong in your valuation multiple, not in your news alerts.
  • Slow rows are iron ore leases and carbon intensity. They change over years. Leases are slowly sorting companies into ore-haves and ore-have-nots; carbon is slowly becoming a cost line through Europe's border tax and India's own carbon market.
  • Cyclical is debt-funded capex. Harmless in a boom, lethal in a bust. This is the row to check against each company's balance sheet.
  • Two-sided is policy swings. The same government that imposed an export duty in 2022 to cap the boom imposed a safeguard duty in 2025 to cushion the bust. Either can move margins overnight, in either direction.
  • Recurring is rail and port logistics: a seasonal irritant that dents a quarter's volumes, rarely a thesis-breaker.

The so-what line below compresses the table into one idea: China and coking coal set the ceiling and floor of margins, while policy and debt decide who is still standing at the bottom.

c8.story:
In Indian steel, the government plays three roles at once: owner, referee and occasional player. It owns SAIL and NMDC. It writes the trade rules. And it can, and does, intervene directly in prices when they get too hot or too cold.

The live rule that matters most today is the safeguard duty on flat steel imports. A safeguard duty is a special kind of tariff, allowed under global trade rules when a sudden surge of imports seriously hurts a domestic industry, regardless of whether those imports are being dumped below cost. The trade remedies directorate, DGTR, investigated the import surge of 2024, a provisional duty began in April 2025, and the finance ministry notified a definitive three-year duty at the end of 2025, stepping down slightly each year. Stainless steel was left out. That duty is the floor under today's domestic coil prices, and its scheduled taper and eventual expiry are dates every steel investor should have on a calendar.

The government's other big lever is the opposite: export duties. In May 2022, with domestic prices high and inflation biting, it taxed steel and iron ore exports, effectively forcing steel to stay at home and cool the price. It withdrew them in November. That episode is the reason why every steel boom in India carries an invisible cap: if prices rise too far, Delhi may step in.

Then the slower rules. Quality control orders from the standards bureau block substandard imports. A production-linked incentive scheme supports specialty and coated steel. The Ministry of Mines decides who owns ore. And carbon is moving from talk to cost: Europe's border tax now charges on imported steel, India's carbon credit trading scheme is setting emission-intensity targets for plants, and the Ministry of Steel has published a definition of green steel that tomorrow's buyers may pay a premium for.
c8.read:
Each row is a regulator or rule. Read across: who it is, what it does, why an investor should care, and its status. Then sort the rows by status, because that is how you prioritise them.

  • Live: the DGTR safeguard and anti-dumping duties, the BIS quality orders and the specialty steel incentive. These are shaping prices and capacity now. The safeguard row is the one to follow week to week; its why column calls its renewal the big date.
  • Always: the Ministry of Steel, the export duty powers and the Ministry of Mines. Permanent fixtures. The export duty row deserves a second look, because it is the government's brake on booms, and it has been used before.
  • New: the EU carbon border tax, which began charging in 2026. Its why column flags the risk: Europe is a key outlet for Indian coil.
  • Coming: the carbon credit trading scheme. It will reward electric furnaces and penalise older blast furnaces, which over time favours the secondary producers and the majors' newer, cleaner capacity.

A useful habit: for each company you own, tick which rows touch it. A blast-furnace exporter touches almost every row. A pipe converter touches few beyond quality orders and project policy, which is part of why its profit bar on card one reads high.

Dated regulatory news for steel, filtered from our feed, sits on the Picks and signals tab.

c9.story:
Michael Porter's five forces framework asks one blunt question: once the money comes in, who gets to keep it? Five groups are trying to take it away from you: rivals, suppliers, customers, newcomers and substitutes.

Run the steel producers through it. Rivalry is intense, and not just among Indian mills: the real rival is the Chinese export price. Suppliers are powerful, because a handful of Australian mines supply most of the coking coal and there is no domestic alternative of the same quality. Customers are a mixed bag: carmakers and large contractors negotiate hard and buy on annual contracts, but the scattered small builders buying rebar have little clout.

Two forces work in the producers' favour. New entrants face a brutal barrier: a blast furnace costs a fortune, takes years to build and needs ore and coal security. And steel has very few substitutes. You cannot build a bridge or a car body out of much else; aluminium and plastics nibble at the edges in autos and pipes, but steel's position is secure.

The converters and specialists have a different profile. Their rivalry is fought through project bids, which is competitive but not a price war against the whole world. Their suppliers are the same few domestic steel majors, a real dependency. But their customers, a refinery buying seamless tubes, a gas company buying line pipe, need certified suppliers, and only a few can qualify. That softens buyer power considerably. On the other side, a pipe or wire plant is much cheaper to build than a steel mill, so new entrants are more of a threat.
c9.read:
The radar has five spokes, one per force. The further a shape reaches along a spoke, the more pressure that force puts on the business, so a smaller shape is the better business.

Two shapes are drawn: integrated and secondary producers, and converters and specialty. Look at their overall size first. The producer shape bulges out towards rivalry and suppliers, both scored two and a half out of three. The converter shape is smaller on those spokes and much smaller on buyers.

Then look for where the shapes cross. On new entrants the producers score just one, because almost nobody can afford to build a blast furnace from scratch, while converters score two, because pipe and wire plants are cheap enough for newcomers. On substitutes the producers score a mere half and converters one, since aluminium and plastic compete harder with pipes than with steel in general. Those crossing points are the honest caveats: the producers are protected by their size, and the converters are more exposed to a new competitor setting up next door.

The table beside the chart gives each score from zero to three with a one-line reason. If you think a particular company deviates, say a producer with its own ore and therefore a much weaker supplier spoke, redraw its shape in your head. That is exactly how the framework is meant to be used.

The so-what underneath puts it in one image: the importer of coking coal is always partly working for Queensland.

c10.story:
A steel company's results call can feel like an engineering lecture: blast furnace relines, pellet plant commissioning, coke rate, hot metal yields. Most of it can be compressed into eight numbers, which you can read in five minutes.

Start with EBITDA per tonne. It is the spread, the cycle and the company's cost position all in one. Compare it with last quarter, with peers, and with the boom years, and you know where the company and the industry stand. Then sales volume: is new capacity filling, and is the company growing at least as fast as Indian demand? A company growing slower than the market is losing share, however good its margins look.

Next, the two numbers that make up the spread: coking coal cost per tonne and realisation per tonne. Coal cost tells you what is coming through the pipeline, since today's purchases are next quarter's melt. Realisation tells you what the company actually got paid after discounts, which can diverge from the headline price lists in a weak market.

Then the balance sheet trio. Net debt to EBITDA tells you whether the expansion is survivable in a bust. Capex to depreciation tells you how hard the company is building. And capital work in progress as a share of the gross block tells you how much of the company's money is sitting in half-built plants, not yet earning.

Finally, return on capital employed. It is the verdict: over a full cycle, did all those furnaces and rolling mills earn more than they cost to fund? Indian steel's history has plenty of expansions that did not.
c10.read:
The table has one row per number. Read across: the number, what it tells you, what good looks like, and today's industry median.

  • What it tells you is the question to ask of each company. For steel, the questions cluster into three groups: the spread (EBITDA per tonne, coal cost, realisation), growth (volume), and survival (debt, capex, work in progress, ROCE).
  • What good looks like is the benchmark, and it is the only column on the page with figures. Treat these as rules of thumb. Notice that the EBITDA per tonne row gives two thresholds: one for a good year and a higher one that signals a boom.
  • Today's industry median comes from the latest filings of the listed companies in our database. Where a metric needs plant-level data our filings do not carry, such as coal cost or realisation per tonne, the median is blank and you will need the companies' investor presentations.

Note that some rows use a stand-in measure from the filings: the EBITDA per tonne row, for example, shows the EBITDA margin, because tonnage is not in the standard accounts. The direction is what matters.

The best way to use the table is a three-way comparison for each company: its own number, the industry median and the good mark. In steel, the debt row deserves special respect. A company with a median-looking margin and a well-below-median debt ratio is the one that gets to buy assets at the bottom of the next cycle.

c11.story:
The most useful warnings about Indian steel rarely come from Indian steel companies. They come from a Chinese housing-starts release, an Australian coal price screen, a DGTR notification, a weekly price survey from Mumbai traders, a customs import table.

Each signal speaks with a different lead. A duty change moves prices the week it lands. Weekly coil and rebar surveys tell you the realisation for the quarter you are already in. Chinese export prices take about a quarter to show up in Indian coil, coking coal bought today is melted next quarter, released government capex becomes rebar orders a few months later, and rising import data warns of price pressure ahead. Furthest out sits Chinese property starts: weak construction in China today is extra steel looking for a home abroad two quarters from now.

Fold those into one rule. Steel is in a genuine up-cycle when three things happen together: Chinese export prices are rising, domestic spreads are widening over coking coal, and imports are falling. Two out of three is early recovery. One out of three is merely a duty-propped rally.

Today two of the three are ticking. Spreads are wider because the duty holds up prices while coal is moderate, and imports are falling because the duty works. The missing sign is the one India cannot control: Chinese prices, still low and stable. That is why the call favours names with their own ore and low debt, and converters with long project order books, over debt-heavy blast-furnace expansion. A rally built on a duty is real, but it lasts only as long as the duty.

A duty wall can hold up prices. Only China can lift them.
c11.read:
The chart places each outside signal along a line by how far ahead it speaks. The further right a dot, the earlier the warning. Hover a dot to see the channel through which it reaches steel earnings.

  • At the far left, same quarter: weekly coil and rebar price surveys, and DGTR notices. These tell you what is happening now.
  • In the middle, one quarter ahead: Chinese export prices, Australian coking coal, government capex releases and steel import data. This is the crowded part of the chart, and it is where most of a steel quarter is decided in advance.
  • Furthest right, two quarters ahead: Chinese property starts, the earliest warning on the chart.

Use the chart as a reading order. Each quarter, start with the right-hand dot, then check the middle cluster: if coal is up and Chinese prices are flat, next quarter's spread narrows, whatever the company says on its call.

Below the chart is the rule with its three signs. A tick means the sign is on, a cross means it is not, and the note gives today's state. For steel: a cross on Chinese export prices, low and stable; a tick on spreads, thanks to the duty floor and moderate coal; a tick on imports falling, because the safeguard is working. Two ticks, one cross: early recovery.

The call box gives the directional view, three supporting points and the three things that would change it: the duty lapsing while China keeps exporting, a coking coal spike, or a squeeze in government capex. Set an alert for each.
